clips.8434cf27aba9: A Kodolab lesson in 5 parts: A polar molecule, Hydrogen bonds, Specific heat, Why ice floats, and The universal solvent.
clips.467c8eff3df7: One end is slightly negative, the other slightly positive.
clips.bafe20da0850: Two lone pairs on oxygen push the hydrogens together, bending the molecule.
clips.770280bb74fd: Bent, its charged ends cannot cancel, so water is polar.
clips.1bbc5398e6b9: Straight C O 2 cancels out and is not.
clips.f0f8ce973bf9: Here is one water molecule, seen from the front.
clips.48134ae493b5: The red sphere at the top is the oxygen.
clips.cb6c62668e1f: The two white spheres below it are hydrogens.
clips.724b9755678d: The two bonds meet at an angle of 104.5 degrees, so the molecule is bent.
clips.394484a5d843: A shared pair of electrons creates a strong bond.
clips.b035518999b7: Shared unevenly, so it is a polar covalent bond.
clips.9718d42b2393: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer than hydrogen can.
clips.ae1df2ad5fce: That leaves this end of the molecule slightly negative.
clips.79b1242a58fd: Each hydrogen has its one electron pulled away by the oxygen.
clips.05a074b69d32: The exposed proton leaves this end slightly positive.
clips.7bafb0b89005: To turn the molecule yourself, press Tab until you reach the model, then use the arrow keys.
clips.0f757ba9c392: Press Space for the next step.
clips.9a94d6a1ef23: The partial positive hydrogen of one water is pulled toward the partial negative oxygen of the next.
clips.f84ad7dd0fb6: That pull is a hydrogen bond.
clips.046279d85eff: Add water and watch the partial positive hydrogens find partial negative oxygens.
clips.48d4a207511c: Every bond breaks and reforms with a new partner, over and over.
clips.477d60107433: Each one is drawn as a dashed line, from the partial positive hydrogen of one molecule to the partial negative oxygen of the next.
clips.16526c0204a8: Press Add Water a few times to build a crowd.
clips.79e066158881: I will tell you how the bonds change.
clips.bc7139c48bc5: Water resists heating, because heat must break its hydrogen bonds first.
clips.1ec8e56552ac: Heat you add goes first into pulling hydrogen bonds apart, not into speeding molecules up.
clips.31189a89b65d: So a lot of heat buys only a small rise in temperature.
clips.aed66da2ae73: Drag the temperature up and watch the network loosen before the molecules visibly speed up.
clips.1d0e3b1cd5f8: Press the up arrow to heat the water, and I will tell you what changes.
clips.e0dfd817e455: Unlike almost every substance, water is less dense as a solid.
clips.6ac3a08fa952: Cool the water until it freezes, then compare the spacing to the liquid’s.
clips.52461ba54c88: Because ice floats, a lake freezes from the top down, and the ice insulates the water beneath where life survives the winter.
clips.94f0d84b4961: Because water is polar, it dissolves ionic and polar substances extraordinarily well.
clips.63e9775e7693: Which end of each water turns toward sodium ion, and which toward chloride ion?
clips.7a23ce6e0929: Then watch the freezing and boiling points move.
clips.04bef733a617: Every cell’s chemistry happens dissolved in water.
clips.9d389c8ec68d: Nonpolar oil has no charge for water to grab, so it stays out, and that is what lets a membrane hold together.
clips.413740a29570: That is the end of the lesson.
